Trump slashes $810M in federal funds.
Evidence: Budget recision, ICE enforcement, Restaurant closures
#Aletheia #USPol

The administration claims the $810 million cut targets wasteful spending and foreign aid without harming legal citizens.
Stated Judgement: (+0.6, +0.5) — Trustworthy / Constructive

In reality, the pocket rescissions and aggressive ICE enforcement disrupt legal asylum frameworks, devastate local small businesses, and inflict sudden collateral harm.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.75, -0.80) — Lesser Evil / Co-optation

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception.
An administrative budget maneuver is framed as fiscal discipline while upending regional economies and immigrant communities.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 13.5, z: 4)

- Federal Budget Action: COND (-0.70, -0.75) — Legal pocket recissions bypass Congress.
- Economic Impact: FAIL (-0.80, -0.85) — Latino eateries face closures.
President Trump utilized pocket rescissions to cancel $810 million in congressionally approved spending, coinciding with heightened immigration enforcement.

The Bright Side:
Exposing fiscal friction forces transparent legislative debates on executive budget authority.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing WHAT (fiscal auditing) with WHO (targeting immigrant communities and small businesses), substituting administrative power for systemic reform.

Social Physics Analysis:
The administration executes a smart selfish maneuver: leveraging budget cuts and enforcement as pretexts to project strength while shifting economic burdens onto vulnerable immigrant workers and small business owners.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil. F_net = S_i*A_i - O_i*A_i, yielding strong negative moral vectors under high systemic strain.

The Unavoidable Truth: Executive budget maneuvers can bypass gridlock but devastate local economies dependent on immigrant labor.

The Unavoidable Lie: Slashing funds labeled as waste carries zero collateral damage for law-abiding communities.

Alethekanon:
Executive power is systematically weaponized under fiscal pretexts, masking structural displacement behind administrative discipline.

Families and small business owners who built honest lives are left devastated by sudden policy shifts and fear.

Playing games with the budget while real restaurants and workers take the hit is wild politics.

Actual Article Body:
Thursday on CNN’s “OutFront,” political commentator Van Jones said President Donald Trump’s “ability to influence anybody outside his little cult has evaporated.”

Host Erin Burnett said, “And I want to ask you about Talarico because obviously Trump’s picking on something there, Van, which is true. Talarico has been off the campaign trail for several days. And Trump you know, trying to get into that. And now Talarico said he had the flu. He came out and did a Zoom or something about that. Does that have an impact though, him having been off the trail?”

Jones said, “Look, Trump doing all his little stuff is not going to make any difference at all. Him being mad at Democrats is ten years old. I do think that Talarico being off the trail isn’t great because he’s very effective on the trail. And when you’re on the trail and you’re in a room with 100 people, and they like what they hear and they post something, and they go in their WhatsApp group, it spreads. So every day you’re not on the trail, you’re missing those opportunities to keep growing. And so, you know, I had the flu last week. And by the way, if you have not gotten your flu shot, get your flu shot. This flu is serious. But, you know, 12 days is a long time. But whatever Trump says about it is —Trump’s ability to influence anybody outside his little cult has evaporated. And so he can say whatever he wants to say.”

Trump to rip Hochul over immigration at Syracuse rally after NYPD detective stabbing, Bronx ICE shooting

President Trump is expected to tear into Gov. Kathy Hochul over the brutal stabbing of an off-duty cop by illegal immigrants when he rallies with Bruce Blakeman in Syracuse on Friday, The Post has learned.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

WASHINGTON — President Trump is expected to tear into Gov. Kathy Hochul over New York’s “sanctuary” status when he rallies with GOP gubernatorial hopeful Bruce Blakeman in Syracuse on Friday following a pair of violent incidents that have outraged both sides of the immigration debate.

Last week, two illegal immigrants with criminal rap sheets allegedly stabbed an off-duty New York Police Department detective in the Bronx after attempting to rob him.

The suspects, 25-year-old D’Angelo Caraballo and 24-year-old Sneider Mejia Bautista, both Dominican nationals, were nabbed early Wednesday after attempting to hide in a basement in Lynn, Mass.

Caraballo was previously thrown in the slammer for reckless driving, unlawful fleeing from an officer, criminal possession of a loaded firearm, and more.

Local cops released him after his December 2024 arrest.

Meanwhile, Bautista was arrested in October of last year for grand larceny, criminal possession of a weapon, stealing property, and other offenses before being set free after the NYPD opted against enforcing ICE’s detainer.

Then on Thursday afternoon, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers shot and wounded Oscar Belgal, a 28-year-old suspected migrant gang member, while a 5-year-old boy believed to be his son sat in the back of his SUV in the Marble Hill section of the Bronx.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Belgal is suspected of links to the notorious Trinitarios gang and has “a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession.”

“This criminal illegal alien was arrested by the NYPD on December 7, 2023, but was released into the community a few days later by reckless Democrat sanctuary policies that put American lives at risk.”

In August, Hochul signed the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, imposing limits on certain types of statewide cooperation with ICE on civil immigration matters.

“New Yorkers are outraged tonight. Immigrant communities are terrified. And we are demanding answers,” she said in a statement following the the Belgal shooting.

“Tonight, I spoke with President Trump and DHS Secretary Mullin about the shooting in Marble Hill,” the governor added on X. “I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York. I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth.”

Blakeman, Hochul’s Republican challenger who is an underdog in most of the polls, vowed earlier this week to sign an executive order mandating local law enforcement cooperation with ICE if he gets elected Nov. 3.

“The insanity is over, we’re putting New Yorkers first,” the Nassau County executive said, adding that “one of the toughest days” of his tenure “was the day that I had to tell our police and our sheriffs that they could no longer cooperate with ICE because of Kathy Hochul.”

Syracuse and surrounding Onondaga County represent a Democratic-leaning island in bright-red central New York. In addition to Blakeman, Trump will hope Friday’s rally can provide a boost to Republican House candidate Kailee Buller, a former USDA official challenging first-term Democratic incumbent John Mannion.

Ahead of the rally, the Trump administration has highlighted the cases of several illegal immigrants who were nabbed in Syracuse for deranged crimes.

That list includes Hsa Mu Na, accused of sexual exploitation of a minor; Norberto Machado-Rodriguez, who faced accusations of sexual assault; Haikham Phimasone, accused of assult; and Said Ibrahim, accused of cruelty toward a child.

Venezuelan favorite Arempas had to close half its restaurants. Crushed, its owners point to Trump’s immigration crackdown.

The couple acknowledged it’s a tough time for restaurants in general. “But the Latino businesses, we are hit with double the strength."

Actual Article Body:
(Rick Egan | The Salt Lake Tribune) Fidel Arrieta, co-owner of Arempas restaurant, in their downtown Salt Lake City location on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026.

Comment

Add as Preferred Source

Sandy and Fidel Arrieta first started selling empanadas from their home, along State Road 26 between Roy and Ogden, around eight years ago.

When they noticed customers kept coming back, craving another bite of their Venezuelan cuisine, the couple decided to open their first restaurant location in downtown Salt Lake City. Together, they named it Arempas.

Arempas grew steadily, eventually expanding to six locations and becoming one of the most recognized Latino restaurant enterprises in the Wasatch Front. But in the last year, the owners have been forced to close down three of their restaurants — in Orem, South Jordan and Sandy.

Why the “catastrophic” shift in business? They point to the federal immigration crackdown under President Donald Trump.

It’s left some loyal customers afraid to eat out and led to about half their workforce disappearing, either choosing to abandon work out of fear or in some cases, deciding to self-deport.

“We started finding ourselves with empty restaurants,” Fidel Arrieta told The Salt Lake Tribune in Spanish. “It was lethal.”

“In general, Latinos are not eating outside of their homes, and that’s affecting us a lot,” Sandy Arrieta added.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

As far as their employees, she said, “people are scared to work even if they have their documents.”

“We had a wonderful team, really extraordinary, but since last year, it started dropping and dropping,” Fidel Arrieta said.

The drop follows a surge between fall 2018 and summer 2025 that saw Venezuelan immigrants in particular increasingly choosing to move to the suburbs of Salt Lake City, The Associated Press reported last month.

(Rick Egan | The Salt Lake Tribune) Fidel and Sandy Arrieta, owners of Arempas restaurant, at their downtown Salt Lake City location.

(Leah Hogsten | The Salt Lake Tribune) From left, beef, chicken and potato empanadas are among the menu items at Arempas.

The restaurant owners are not alone. The organizers of the Facebook group Utahzolanos, which shares news and builds community among Venezuelans in Utah, told The Tribune they’ve heard from at least 100 Venezuelan families throughout the state in the last year who have either self-deported or are considering it.

“There is a lot of fear in the community, because people thought they were in the country legally — because they had their open asylum case, and because they had employment authorization and were paying taxes,” one of the organizers, Patricia Quiñones, told The Tribune in Spanish.

“But this administration,” she feels, “unfortunately considers anyone without permanent residence ‘illegal,’ and so that has made a lot of families chose self-deportation.”

In 2021 and 2023, Venezuelan immigrants were granted Temporary Protected Status, which allows people who can’t safely return to their home country to work in the U.S. and exempts them from immigration enforcement.

About a year ago, though, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security revoked TPS for Venezuelan immigrants.

Earlier this year, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found DHS did that unlawfully for some Venezuelan and Haitian nationals. But this week, the Supreme Court vacated and returned that ruling for review, in light of a separate case that set new precedent.

Throughout Trump’s second term, immigration enforcement agents have arrested Venezuelans more frequently, according to a Tribune analysis of federal data from 2025.

Since his second inauguration alone, 629 Venezuelan citizens have been detained in Utah and removed by immigration enforcement agents, according to the Deportation Data Project.

At Arempas’ downtown Salt Lake City location, where Sandy Arrieta spoke with The Tribune, she said she calls her workers her “kids.” The closures have left her shaken.

“I didn’t want to leave the house, and it felt like my world was ending, but I told myself, ‘We have to keep going with the other restaurants,’” she said in Spanish.

(Rick Egan | The Salt Lake Tribune) Sandy Arrieta, co-owner of Arempas, at the couple's downtown Salt Lake City location.

(Leah Hogsten | The Salt Lake Tribune) The downtown location is dotted with fachadas, or "facades" — little wooden store and house fronts. Murals and picturesque scenes of Venezuela's Caribbean Coast also fill the eatery.

Here, longtime customers have seemed shocked to learn the couple’s been forced to close three locations, she said.

Before all of this, Arempas’ success peaked around four years ago, including a feature on an episode of Guy Fieri’s “Diners, Drive-ins & Dives” on Food Network in 2021. Around that time, thousands of Venezuelans were arriving in Utah, and the Arrietas started opening more locations.

The downtown restaurant, especially, was “overflowing” with customers, they said in Spanish. Late at night, when other spots had closed for the day, Arempas was one of the only places open and bustling, they said.

“People come into this location with a party vibe, and it’s much more relaxed,” Sandy Arrieta said.

Soon, it could be their only full-service restaurant. Between the challenges they’ve faced, and the shifting economy, the couple may need to shut down their Midvale location, too, she said.

They turned half that restaurant into a bar area about a year ago for parties, karaoke and more — a “creative” way to try and turn extra profit.

They also operate a food truck, which they are working to schedule more often, as well as a shop in Salt Lake Community College’s cafeteria, where they got approval to open last year after the school’s Student Association president, who was Venezuelan, led efforts to bring Venezuelan food to campus.

Fidel Arrieta acknowledged it’s a tough time for restaurants in general.

“But the Latino businesses, we are hit with double the strength,” he said.

Trump says voter fraud is rampant. The evidence says otherwise.

On this week’s “More To The Story,” conservative activist J. Christian Adams is challenged on his claims of widespread voter fraud in the US. Then he abruptly ends the interview.

Actual Article Body:
“I’m not going to engage in a simple-minded, back-and-forth tug-of-war with you over quibbling over numbers and who’s got the moral high ground on this,” conservative activist J. Christian Adams told our host Al Letson before ending the interview.Stephen Maturen/Getty

If you’ve ever listened to President Trump talk about our elections, you might hear something like this: Voter fraud is rampant. Noncitizens are regularly voting illegally. And our elections are rigged. The president often uses the bully pulpit to repeat these claims despite study after study showing they’re just not true. But it’s not just the president. There are many others at the ground level saying the same things to justify voting restrictions that could disenfranchise legal voters, especially voters of color.

One of them is J. Christian Adams. An activist and former trial attorney for the US Department of Justice, Adams was named to Trump’s Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity in 2017. Today, he’s the president of Public Interest Legal Foundation, a nonprofit that advocates for stricter voter ID laws and sues states and local governments to remove illegal voters from election rolls.

On this week’s “More To The Story,” Adams claims there’s systemic voter fraud in the US before abruptly ending the interview after host Al Letson challenges his assertions. Al then talks with Mother Jones National Voting Rights Correspondent Ari Berman about the lack of evidence from activists like Adams, the claims Adams and PILF have made that noncitizens are illegally voting, and what conservative activists who say election fraud is rampant are really trying to achieve.

Thursday on CNN’s “OutFront,” political commentator Van Jones said President Donald Trump’s “ability to influence anybody outside his little cult has evaporated.”

Host Erin Burnett said, “And I want to ask you about Talarico because obviously Trump’s picking on something there, Van, which is true. Talarico has been off the campaign trail for several days. And Trump you know, trying to get into that. And now Talarico said he had the flu. He came out and did a Zoom or something about that. Does that have an impact though, him having been off the trail?”

Jones said, “Look, Trump doing all his little stuff is not going to make any difference at all. Him being mad at Democrats is ten years old. I do think that Talarico being off the trail isn’t great because he’s very effective on the trail. And when you’re on the trail and you’re in a room with 100 people, and they like what they hear and they post something, and they go in their WhatsApp group, it spreads. So every day you’re not on the trail, you’re missing those opportunities to keep growing. And so, you know, I had the flu last week. And by the way, if you have not gotten your flu shot, get your flu shot. This flu is serious. But, you know, 12 days is a long time. But whatever Trump says about it is —Trump’s ability to influence anybody outside his little cult has evaporated. And so he can say whatever he wants to say.”

WASHINGTON — President Trump is expected to tear into Gov. Kathy Hochul over New York’s “sanctuary” status when he rallies with GOP gubernatorial hopeful Bruce Blakeman in Syracuse on Friday following a pair of violent incidents that have outraged both sides of the immigration debate.

Last week, two illegal immigrants with criminal rap sheets allegedly stabbed an off-duty New York Police Department detective in the Bronx after attempting to rob him.

The suspects, 25-year-old D’Angelo Caraballo and 24-year-old Sneider Mejia Bautista, both Dominican nationals, were nabbed early Wednesday after attempting to hide in a basement in Lynn, Mass.

Caraballo was previously thrown in the slammer for reckless driving, unlawful fleeing from an officer, criminal possession of a loaded firearm, and more.

Local cops released him after his December 2024 arrest.

Meanwhile, Bautista was arrested in October of last year for grand larceny, criminal possession of a weapon, stealing property, and other offenses before being set free after the NYPD opted against enforcing ICE’s detainer.

Then on Thursday afternoon, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers shot and wounded Oscar Belgal, a 28-year-old suspected migrant gang member, while a 5-year-old boy believed to be his son sat in the back of his SUV in the Marble Hill section of the Bronx.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Belgal is suspected of links to the notorious Trinitarios gang and has “a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession.”

“This criminal illegal alien was arrested by the NYPD on December 7, 2023, but was released into the community a few days later by reckless Democrat sanctuary policies that put American lives at risk.”

In August, Hochul signed the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, imposing limits on certain types of statewide cooperation with ICE on civil immigration matters.

“New Yorkers are outraged tonight. Immigrant communities are terrified. And we are demanding answers,” she said in a statement following the the Belgal shooting.

“Tonight, I spoke with President Trump and DHS Secretary Mullin about the shooting in Marble Hill,” the governor added on X. “I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York. I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth.”

Blakeman, Hochul’s Republican challenger who is an underdog in most of the polls, vowed earlier this week to sign an executive order mandating local law enforcement cooperation with ICE if he gets elected Nov. 3.

“The insanity is over, we’re putting New Yorkers first,” the Nassau County executive said, adding that “one of the toughest days” of his tenure “was the day that I had to tell our police and our sheriffs that they could no longer cooperate with ICE because of Kathy Hochul.”

Syracuse and surrounding Onondaga County represent a Democratic-leaning island in bright-red central New York. In addition to Blakeman, Trump will hope Friday’s rally can provide a boost to Republican House candidate Kailee Buller, a former USDA official challenging first-term Democratic incumbent John Mannion.

Ahead of the rally, the Trump administration has highlighted the cases of several illegal immigrants who were nabbed in Syracuse for deranged crimes.

That list includes Hsa Mu Na, accused of sexual exploitation of a minor; Norberto Machado-Rodriguez, who faced accusations of sexual assault; Haikham Phimasone, accused of assult; and Said Ibrahim, accused of cruelty toward a child.

Actual Article Body:
(Rick Egan | The Salt Lake Tribune) Fidel Arrieta, co-owner of Arempas restaurant, in their downtown Salt Lake City location on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026.

Comment

Sandy and Fidel Arrieta first started selling empanadas from their home, along State Road 26 between Roy and Ogden, around eight years ago.

When they noticed customers kept coming back, craving another bite of their Venezuelan cuisine, the couple decided to open their first restaurant location in downtown Salt Lake City. Together, they named it Arempas.

Arempas grew steadily, eventually expanding to six locations and becoming one of the most recognized Latino restaurant enterprises in the Wasatch Front. But in the last year, the owners have been forced to close down three of their restaurants — in Orem, South Jordan and Sandy.

Why the “catastrophic” shift in business? They point to the federal immigration crackdown under President Donald Trump.

It’s left some loyal customers afraid to eat out and led to about half their workforce disappearing, either choosing to abandon work out of fear or in some cases, deciding to self-deport.

“We started finding ourselves with empty restaurants,” Fidel Arrieta told The Salt Lake Tribune in Spanish. “It was lethal.”

“In general, Latinos are not eating outside of their homes, and that’s affecting us a lot,” Sandy Arrieta added.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

As far as their employees, she said, “people are scared to work even if they have their documents.”

“We had a wonderful team, really extraordinary, but since last year, it started dropping and dropping,” Fidel Arrieta said.

The drop follows a surge between fall 2018 and summer 2025 that saw Venezuelan immigrants in particular increasingly choosing to move to the suburbs of Salt Lake City, The Associated Press reported last month.

(Rick Egan | The Salt Lake Tribune) Fidel and Sandy Arrieta, owners of Arempas restaurant, at their downtown Salt Lake City location.

(Leah Hogsten | The Salt Lake Tribune) From left, beef, chicken and potato empanadas are among the menu items at Arempas.

The restaurant owners are not alone. The organizers of the Facebook group Utahzolanos, which shares news and builds community among Venezuelans in Utah, told The Tribune they’ve heard from at least 100 Venezuelan families throughout the state in the last year who have either self-deported or are considering it.

“There is a lot of fear in the community, because people thought they were in the country legally — because they had their open asylum case, and because they had employment authorization and were paying taxes,” one of the organizers, Patricia Quiñones, told The Tribune in Spanish.

“But this administration,” she feels, “unfortunately considers anyone without permanent residence ‘illegal,’ and so that has made a lot of families chose self-deportation.”

In 2021 and 2023, Venezuelan immigrants were granted Temporary Protected Status, which allows people who can’t safely return to their home country to work in the U.S. and exempts them from immigration enforcement.

About a year ago, though, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security revoked TPS for Venezuelan immigrants.

Earlier this year, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found DHS did that unlawfully for some Venezuelan and Haitian nationals. But this week, the Supreme Court vacated and returned that ruling for review, in light of a separate case that set new precedent.

Throughout Trump’s second term, immigration enforcement agents have arrested Venezuelans more frequently, according to a Tribune analysis of federal data from 2025.

Since his second inauguration alone, 629 Venezuelan citizens have been detained in Utah and removed by immigration enforcement agents, according to the Deportation Data Project.

At Arempas’ downtown Salt Lake City location, where Sandy Arrieta spoke with The Tribune, she said she calls her workers her “kids.” The closures have left her shaken.

“I didn’t want to leave the house, and it felt like my world was ending, but I told myself, ‘We have to keep going with the other restaurants,’” she said in Spanish.

(Rick Egan | The Salt Lake Tribune) Sandy Arrieta, co-owner of Arempas, at the couple's downtown Salt Lake City location.

(Leah Hogsten | The Salt Lake Tribune) The downtown location is dotted with fachadas, or "facades" — little wooden store and house fronts. Murals and picturesque scenes of Venezuela's Caribbean Coast also fill the eatery.

Here, longtime customers have seemed shocked to learn the couple’s been forced to close three locations, she said.

Before all of this, Arempas’ success peaked around four years ago, including a feature on an episode of Guy Fieri’s “Diners, Drive-ins & Dives” on Food Network in 2021. Around that time, thousands of Venezuelans were arriving in Utah, and the Arrietas started opening more locations.

The downtown restaurant, especially, was “overflowing” with customers, they said in Spanish. Late at night, when other spots had closed for the day, Arempas was one of the only places open and bustling, they said.

“People come into this location with a party vibe, and it’s much more relaxed,” Sandy Arrieta said.

Soon, it could be their only full-service restaurant. Between the challenges they’ve faced, and the shifting economy, the couple may need to shut down their Midvale location, too, she said.

They turned half that restaurant into a bar area about a year ago for parties, karaoke and more — a “creative” way to try and turn extra profit.

They also operate a food truck, which they are working to schedule more often, as well as a shop in Salt Lake Community College’s cafeteria, where they got approval to open last year after the school’s Student Association president, who was Venezuelan, led efforts to bring Venezuelan food to campus.

Fidel Arrieta acknowledged it’s a tough time for restaurants in general.

“But the Latino businesses, we are hit with double the strength,” he said.

Trump says voter fraud is rampant. The evidence says otherwise.

On this week’s “More To The Story,” conservative activist J. Christian Adams is challenged on his claims of widespread voter fraud in the US. Then he abruptly ends the interview.

Actual Article Body:
“I’m not going to engage in a simple-minded, back-and-forth tug-of-war with you over quibbling over numbers and who’s got the moral high ground on this,” conservative activist J. Christian Adams told our host Al Letson before ending the interview.Stephen Maturen/Getty

If you’ve ever listened to President Trump talk about our elections, you might hear something like this: Voter fraud is rampant. Noncitizens are regularly voting illegally. And our elections are rigged. The president often uses the bully pulpit to repeat these claims despite study after study showing they’re just not true. But it’s not just the president. There are many others at the ground level saying the same things to justify voting restrictions that could disenfranchise legal voters, especially voters of color.

One of them is J. Christian Adams. An activist and former trial attorney for the US Department of Justice, Adams was named to Trump’s Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity in 2017. Today, he’s the president of Public Interest Legal Foundation, a nonprofit that advocates for stricter voter ID laws and sues states and local governments to remove illegal voters from election rolls.

On this week’s “More To The Story,” Adams claims there’s systemic voter fraud in the US before abruptly ending the interview after host Al Letson challenges his assertions. Al then talks with Mother Jones National Voting Rights Correspondent Ari Berman about the lack of evidence from activists like Adams, the claims Adams and PILF have made that noncitizens are illegally voting, and what conservative activists who say election fraud is rampant are really trying to achieve.
